headline: Hot Take Arena: Speaking and Debate for ESL Classes
problemStatement: Opinion activities can stop at a quick vote, leaving learners with little reason to support an idea. Hot Take Arena moves from choosing a side to explaining it aloud. Students respond to a statement, hear counter-arguments, and can see whether the conversation changes anyone's view.
outcomes: Practice giving a clear opinion and supporting it with a reason or example.
Listen and respond to an opposing view without turning disagreement into a personal argument.
Use sentence starters and fair speaking turns to develop debate fluency.
howItWorks: Select Full debate, Quick take, or Wild card. Full debate begins with students choosing Agree or Disagree and gives speakers turns from both sides.
The teacher can invite a smart devil's advocate to challenge the arguments on either side. At the end, the class votes again and reviews how opinions shifted.
Quick take asks students to choose a side and submit one reason on their phones before the teacher reveals and discusses the responses.
Wild card deals each student a Defend or Attack side on their phone for an absurd statement. Students speak in turns, then the class votes on which side argued better.
teacherUseCases: Use Full debate when a unit question has more than one defensible answer and you want students to hear both positions.
Choose Quick take for a shorter speaking check, or Wild card when playful prompts can help learners try arguments without personal stakes.

faq.q: What is the difference between the three modes?
faq.a: Full debate includes opening and closing votes with spoken turns. Quick take collects a side and a reason. Wild card assigns Defend or Attack positions for an absurd prompt.

faq.q: How does the activity keep the debate balanced?
faq.a: Full debate alternates the next suggested speaker between Agree and Disagree. The teacher can still call any raised hand, and a devil's advocate can challenge both sides.

faq.q: Do students have to type their argument?
faq.a: In Quick take, each student sends one reason from a phone. Full debate and Wild card focus on spoken arguments, with phones carrying the assigned side and sentence starters in Wild card.
After Full debate, students vote again. The result shows the before-and-after balance and who switched sides, giving the class a concrete reason to discuss persuasive evidence.
